title: AI-Assisted Hackers Target Indian Fintechs on Weekends, CERT-In Warns of Escalation
excerpt: CERT-In has named the actor CRAFTY FALCON in a critical advisory, saying attackers use AI tools to abuse victims' own payment APIs, steal crypto wallet keys and return to firms even after they tried to fix earlier breaches.
body:
• CERT-In warns of a significant escalation in attacks by an AI-assisted actor it calls CRAFTY FALCON, targeting Indian lenders, fintechs, payment providers and crypto exchanges.
  • Attackers exploit exposed test and development systems and APIs, rewrite victim applications to make unauthorised payment calls, and start with tiny test transfers before larger thefts.
  • Attacks are timed for holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows, and some firms were re-targeted after incomplete remediation.
  • If you use Indian fintech, lending or crypto apps, enable transaction alerts, review beneficiaries and treat unexpected small test credits or debits as a warning sign to check with the provider.

India's Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-In, has warned the financial services industry of a significant escalation in attacks by an AI-assisted financial threat actor that has re-targeted victims after they flubbed remediation efforts, The Register reported.

CERT-In first detected the attacks in October and issued an advisory warning digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers and wallet operators that attackers were targeting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints. If attackers found a way in, they tried to use payment APIs to steal money.

In an update published this week, CERT-In said it continues to hear of successful attacks, including from outfits that tried to remediate their systems after earlier incidents. CERT-In rated its November 4 warning critical and named the actor CRAFTY FALCON, BeInCrypto reported.

Timed for when defenders aren't watching

"The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response," CERT-In warned, in the passage quoted by The Register.

CERT-In also revealed that the crew uses AI-enhanced tools including the ARTEX penetration-testing tool, the Cairn attack search engine and the CyberStrikeAI framework. BeInCrypto additionally listed PentAGI among the publicly available AI tools found in the attacks, saying the tools can run attack chains and adjust payloads as targets respond.

How the intrusions work

CRAFTY FALCON looks for internet-exposed environments used for testing or development, where it finds artefacts such as shared credentials, tokens or network paths that help it move into production systems, according to The Register.

If it gets in, the crew rewrites victims' applications so they make unauthorised API calls. Because victims' defences assume only legitimate apps would call those APIs, activity conducted by the rewritten apps is not flagged as an attack. CERT-In said the actor also creates many functionally identical variants in rapid succession, a pattern it described as consistent with AI-generated code.

Once it has a foothold, the crew makes tiny test payments of about $0.01 to check whether its attacks work, The Register reported. If those transfers succeed, it makes larger payments. When the target is a cryptocurrency exchange or virtual digital asset service provider, the crew steals wallet keys and empties cryptocurrency wallets, both outlets reported. CERT-In has not named any affected firm or disclosed how much was lost.

What CERT-In wants firms to do

CERT-In warned the attacks are active and escalating and therefore worthy of round-the-clock monitoring. Its advice includes improving logging, monitoring for anomalies in real time and alerting, keeping test environments off the internet, and restricting access to cloud resources, according to The Register.

For crypto platforms, BeInCrypto reported, CERT-In wants wallet keys stored in hardware security modules or cold custody, multi-signature approval for crypto withdrawals, and cooling periods for new beneficiaries across payment systems.

For the diaspora, many of whom move money through Indian fintech, lending and crypto apps, the practical lesson is vigilance rather than panic: keep transaction alerts on, review payees and beneficiaries in your apps, and question any unfamiliar small transfer, because in this campaign a tiny test payment was the step before a larger theft.
